expectedFacts: The first downstream route is processed first; its response body is read as a string and parsed with JToken.Parse.

For each later route whose key has a matching route-keys config entry, the configured JSON path is applied with SelectTokens, distinct values are taken, and one downstream call is made per distinct value.
For each call, a placeholder named after the configured parameter and holding the extracted value is added to a copy of the request's placeholder list, which is stored on the cloned request context.
DownstreamPathPlaceholderReplacer.Replace substitutes each placeholder name with its value inside the downstream path template.

The header name is the route's RequestIdKey, falling back to the default 'RequestId' key; if the client sent that header, its first value becomes HttpContext.TraceIdentifier, otherwise the existing TraceIdentifier stays.
ExceptionHandlerMiddleware applies the same idea earlier using the global configuration's request-id key.

The identifier is added as a header to the downstream request only when the downstream route's own RequestIdKey is non-empty, the value is non-empty, and that header is not already present; the fallback default key alone is not forwarded.

r3-ocelot-17.query: How long does the gateway wait for a backend to reply when nothing is configured, and what happens if one of the explicitly listed routes sets the waiting time to zero or a negative number?
expectedFacts: The default timeout is 90 seconds (DefTimeout); the static DefaultTimeoutSeconds setter falls back to 90 if assigned a value below 3.
CreateTimeout evaluates route.Timeout.Positive(default) ?? global.Timeout.Positive(default) ?? default; Positive returns null for null, the value if above zero, otherwise the default.
So a zero or negative route timeout becomes the default timeout (90 seconds unless changed) directly; it does not fall through to the global timeout (only a missing route timeout does).

The gateway does not compare body size with a limit itself; it reacts to an exception raised while sending: an HttpRequestException (or TimeoutException) whose inner exception is a BadHttpRequestException with status 413 becomes a PayloadTooLargeError.
PayloadTooLargeError is created with status 413 (RequestEntityTooLarge), and ErrorsToHttpStatusCodeMapper returns 413 Payload Too Large when the errors contain the PayloadTooLargeError code.
Other HttpRequestExceptions map to ConnectionToDownstreamServiceError (502 Bad Gateway), except the invalid non-ASCII header case, which maps to a 400 BadRequestError.
